title: Wall Street Just Raised India's Growth Forecast to 7% — the Sharpest Upward Revision in Over a Year
excerpt: Bank of America, Crisil, and Goldman Sachs have all upgraded India's outlook in the span of a week, citing collapsing oil prices, the Iran peace deal, and a capex surge — while the rupee posts its first quarterly gain since early 2025
body:
Three of the most closely watched names in global finance have upgraded India's growth outlook within the same week — and the collective message is unusually clear: India's macro story has turned a corner.

Bank of America Securities raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast for India to 7 per cent, up sharply from 6.2 per cent in April. Crisil, India's leading domestic rating agency, revised its estimate to 6.5 per cent. And Goldman Sachs lifted its projection by 30 basis points, while simultaneously lowering its inflation forecast by 20 basis points and now expecting India to run a balance of payments surplus of 0.7 per cent of GDP.

For NRI investors and the diaspora watching India's economic trajectory, this marks one of the most concentrated waves of positive revisions since the pandemic recovery.

## What Changed

The upgrades converge on three factors that have shifted dramatically since April.

**Oil.** Brent crude has collapsed from over $120 a barrel at the peak of the Iran-related disruption to approximately $71 — a level not seen since before the US-Israeli-Iran conflict erupted in late February. Bank of America now projects Brent will average $72 in the second half of 2026 and $65 in 2027, assuming the fragile West Asia peace holds. For India, the world's third-largest oil importer, every $10 drop in crude saves roughly 0.4 per cent of GDP on the import bill and eases inflationary pressure.

**The peace dividend.** The US-Iran interim deal, brokered through Qatari mediation, has reopened Strait of Hormuz shipping lanes and taken the geopolitical risk premium out of energy markets. Goldman Sachs explicitly cited this as the driver behind its revised outlook, noting that the macro backdrop for India "has improved materially."

**Government spending.** Domestic capex has surged. Government capital expenditure grew 38.7 per cent year-on-year in May, with 17 major Indian states reporting a combined 44.7 per cent jump. Infrastructure and construction goods output rose 6.3 per cent — evidence that the investment cycle, which had stalled during the oil shock, is regaining momentum.

## The Rupee's Quiet Recovery

Perhaps the most telling signal of India's improved positioning is the rupee itself.

The currency logged its first quarterly gain in five quarters in the April-June period, recovering from a record low of nearly 97 per dollar in May to settle around 94.50–94.66 at the quarter's close. It was among the best-performing Asian currencies in June.

The recovery was supported not just by oil, but by a volley of Reserve Bank of India policy measures designed to attract dollar inflows — including liberalised bond investment windows and incentives for foreign holders of Indian government debt.

Analysts at Commerzbank now expect USD/INR to consolidate in the 94–96 range, with a possible shift to 92–94 if oil prices fall further. A Reuters poll of 44 strategists forecasts the rupee at 94.5 in three months and 95 by year-end.

"Factoring in a positive sentiment effect as oil prices have come off and the capital account pressure will also ease with dollar flows coming in from the measures that the RBI announced," said Sakshi Gupta, principal economist at HDFC Bank. "We are expecting a stable movement for the rupee with a mild appreciation bias."

## The Caveats

The upgrades come with clear caveats.

Bank of America is forecasting 75 basis points of Federal Reserve rate hikes starting September 2026 — a scenario that would tighten global financial conditions and pull capital away from emerging markets, including India. Foreign investors have already sold more than $29 billion of Indian equities this year, and the rupee remains down 5.4 per cent against the dollar for the year.

The Index of Industrial Production slipped to 1.2 per cent in May — its lowest since August 2024 — with weakness in pharmaceuticals, chemicals, and textiles. And India's manufacturing PMI, while still expansionary at 54, hit a near four-year low in June. The upgrades reflect the oil-driven macro windfall; the earnings cycle has yet to catch up.

"India is not a low-growth or broken story, but it is a market where valuations remain relatively full," said Ninghui Liu, head of APAC investment strategy at State Street, which manages $5.6 trillion. "The bar for increasing allocation is quite clear: we need to see sustained earnings recovery coming through."

## What It Means for NRI Investors

For NRIs with India-linked portfolios, the near-term picture has distinctly improved.

Rupee stability means dollar-denominated returns on Indian equity and debt holdings are no longer being eroded by currency depreciation — a major headwind in the first quarter. The Nifty 50 has outperformed broader Asian indices in recent sessions, rising 0.71 per cent on Thursday even as South Korea's KOSPI crashed 8 per cent.

But the longer-term case depends on whether earnings growth — which has been stuck in single digits for two fiscal years — can accelerate to the mid-teens, as analysts now project. If it does, India's current valuation premium may begin to look justified. If it does not, the rally may prove fragile.

For now, three of the biggest names in global finance are saying the same thing: the floor has been raised.

**Sources:** *Bank of America Securities (June 30, 2026); Goldman Sachs Research; Crisil; Reuters; The Hindu Business Line; Commerzbank; HDFC Bank Economics*
